interactions.hypothesis: Shared injury makes joint differ from product.
Same-half rivals reduce each other's chance.
Same-surface consecutive events carry form.

Two surface ratings of the same player are drawn from a correlated joint posterior; high covariance raises the probability of winning both and low covariance behaves like independence, so the joint probability depends on a second-moment parameter, not only on means.

The chance of arriving fit at the second leg is the persistence probability reduced by the load of the first; long runs lower fitness but also signal fit state, so the multiplicative load effect is small but measurable.
After a short gap (under three weeks) fatigue and surface transition cost reduce the next leg's chance; beyond about six weeks the carryover disappears, so the link has a threshold in the gap.

For the same-player reading, a high surface covariance raises the probability of a second title given the first mainly when the second leg's field is thin at the top (key rivals absent or injured); against a deep field the covariance matters less because the per-match upset risk dominates, so the covariance effect scales with field concentration.

When a player is injured the combination probability falls to near zero for all his legs at once, while when healthy the legs are close to independent given ratings; the joint is a mixture over health regimes.

combo_tournament_winners.label: Combination tournament-winner markets
combo_tournament_winners.mechanism: Combos require the joint probability across events that share participation and health state and may be mutually exclusive; the joint is not the product of marginals. A joint simulation with a shared player health state and per-event draw gives consistent prices.
combo_tournament_winners.target: Joint outcome of several tournament winners.

interactions.hypothesis: Dependence increases the sweep share and decider share simultaneously relative to independence.
Tired players are less likely to convert a decider, lowering 3-2 wins for them.
Format changes the mapping of the same rating gap to scorelines.

The correlation between sets scales with the size of the favourite's edge: for a large edge a shared form shock raises 2-0 mass more than for an even pair, because the shock moves a larger spread of the pair gap.
Serving first adds an early game lead, and the lead is worth more when break chances are rare; for two big servers the first-server advantage in set win is larger than for return-dominant clay pairs.

Within a pre-match edge bin the straight-set share is not fixed: slower courts and weaker servers lengthen sets and push mass from 2-0 to 2-1 (and from 3-0/3-1 to 3-2), while a very lopsided pair stays near its edge-bin share whatever the pace. The pace effect therefore matters most for mid-edge pairs, giving a conditional rather than additive link.
In best-of-five the dependence between sets compounds across more transitions, so the same latent shock raises 3-0 and 3-2 mass differently than it does in best-of-three.
The rung affected by a retirement depends on when it happens: a retirement before set 2 settles no 2-1 rung while one in set 3 leaves 2-1 open; the regime is set by timing.

exact_set_score.label: Exact set score and match score
exact_set_score.mechanism: Exact set score requires the joint distribution of set outcomes per player; probability mass depends on win probability, between-set dependence and format. Dependence between sets increases 2-0/3-0 sweeps and deciders; the main mispricing risk is in the relative probability of 2-0 vs 2-1 for evenly matched pairs.
exact_set_score.target: Exact final set score (2-0, 2-1, 3-0, 3-1, 3-2) or exact match set pattern.

interactions.hypothesis: Game win probability is nonlinear in spw, so small spw errors matter at deuce.
Latency edge appears as post-score price drift in the tape.
Medical signals reduce a player's spw and raise retirement probability.

Game win probability is a steep function of spw at deuce and break-point scores, so a given posterior error costs more at 30-30 than at 40-0; the value of better spw information is concentrated in the tight scores.
Ball freshness boosts big servers more than baseliners, so the new-ball uplift in hold probability is a multiple of the server's pace advantage and absent for weak servers.
Wind on one end lowers first-serve in-percentage there and makes second serves the key point; the effect appears only in games served into the wind and flips at changeovers.
A medical timeout makes past points less representative of future serving, so the posterior should forget faster than the base update rule; ignoring the break underprices the receiver's break chance.

If a game is cut short by retirement or suspension, the traded event settles differently depending on the point score reached: at 40-0 a rule that credits unconditionally decidable results behaves unlike a rule that voids an incomplete game. The settlement regime therefore switches the effective probability by score state, and matters most at the high-leverage deuce and break-point scores.

game_winner_inplay.label: In-play game winner
game_winner_inplay.mechanism: In-play game markets are dominated by server identity and the point score; the server wins most games. The probability follows closed-form formulas from spw updated with in-match information, while feed latency and break-point luck determine the realised edge.
game_winner_inplay.target: Winner of the current game given live score.

inputs.why: Sets the base probability: a surface-blended Elo gap converts to a win probability, and the surface weighting is what separates a clay specialist from a hard-court player with the same overall rating.

Match odds are really the pair's point-win rates on serve and return; adjusting each player's raw rates for the quality of opponents faced shows how this specific pairing plays, which a single rating hides.
Converts point-level serve/return strength into game, set and match probability through the hold/break chain, so a small per-point edge is amplified in a best-of-five and diluted in a best-of-three.

Best-of-five gives the stronger player more sets to express a per-point edge, so the same rating gap implies a more lopsided winner price than in best-of-three; the contract's format must be known before pricing.
An injured or ill player wins less and may retire; the price moves only when the status is public, so the timestamp of the report matters more than the report itself.
Long previous matches, a short turnaround and late-night finishes lower serve speed and movement; the effect is largest in later rounds and best-of-five events.
Fast courts, altitude and indoor air raise hold rates and favour big servers, while slow clay favours returners and rallying; the effect scales with how different the two players' styles are.

Head-to-head only adds information once serve/return rates and handedness are controlled; a lopsided history with a small sample is mostly noise, but a stylistic mismatch (big server vs elite returner) persists.
Returning, young and low-sample players have wide rating error; the winner price should be shrunk toward 50% less aggressively for them, and the market often over-trusts a single recent result.
Whether a retirement or walkover settles the winner contract as a win, void or loss changes which side is worth buying when one player is hurt; the exact contract wording decides the payoff.
The sportsbook closing line is the efficient-market benchmark; any model must beat it, not just predict outcomes, and its timestamp vs the Kalshi quote determines whether the comparison is fair.

Choosing how to remove the book's margin (proportional, power, Shin) changes the implied probability of longshots by a few points; favourite-longshot bias in tennis lines is exactly where a mispricing study would look.
Raw serve-point and return-point win rates by surface are the building blocks of the pair model; their sample size per surface (few grass matches) limits how far they can be trusted.
Recent results relative to rating expectation capture slumps and hot streaks only if they exceed what rating updates already absorb; most apparent form is regression to the rating.
Break chances come mostly from second-serve points; a player with a weak second serve against a strong returner loses more games than their first-serve numbers imply.
Lets a player's thin clay or grass record borrow information from similar surfaces, which matters most early in the season and for players switching surface.
A left-hander's serve patterns and ad-court slice are unusual to face, and the opponent's lack of practice against them shows in break rates, but the edge is small and shrinks with sample size.
Long-haul travel and time shifts affect the first days of an event; it matters for early rounds after intercontinental swings and is largely gone by the quarterfinals.
Rain delays and overnight suspensions change momentum, order of play and rest, and can leave a match unfinished past the contract's settlement window.
Swaps a three-way categorical surface label for a continuous pace response so the winner price separates specialists at fast vs slow hard courts.
Corrects a systematic scale mismatch that only affects Challenger/lower-tier winner contracts, where Kalshi lists many matches.
Winner contracts on doubles pairs cannot be priced from singles ratings; the dedicated series are listed and their pairs change week to week.
Prevents applying tour-match calibration to exhibitions where effort and format differ from tour rules.
Gives the probability the contract voids to fair price rather than resolving, and flags when a price move reflects a withdrawal.
For the fourteen named-round series the round index and rounds already played set late-round parity and accumulated load for the one fixed pairing; no draw-path use.
Order of play fixes session, not-before time and rest gap for the specific match, shifting conditions and recovery and triggering rain-delay continuation.

interactions.hypothesis: Edge amplification in best-of-five means the same rating gap yields larger win probability.
Match-winner wording typically settles on the progression winner; injury risk changes both performance and the retirement path.
Serve dominance gets more weight on fast event conditions.
Heavy favourites against uncertain-rated opponents are where de-vig bias and rating noise interact most.

A big server's rating gain from court pace multiplies with the event's measured pace index; on a fast indoor court the same server gains several Elo points while a counter-puncher loses them, which the surface label alone cannot represent.
Best-of-five amplifies the favourite's edge, but a shared day-level form shock reduces that amplification; the net direction flips when the shock variance is large relative to the per-point edge.

If a player starts injured, point-win rate falls and retirement probability rises; how the contract treats retirement decides whether that shifts the fair price in the same or opposite direction to the on-court outcome.
Fatigue effects emerge only after long previous matches (about 3 hours or five sets) and are larger in best-of-five, so the response is near zero below a load threshold then steepens.

A player recently promoted from ITF to Challenger carries both a scale offset and a wide rating error, and the two compound: the winner price should shrink toward 50% more for the cross-level pair than for two same-level players.

match_winner.label: Match winner
match_winner.mechanism: Match-win probability is a function of the serve/return point-win edge on the actual surface, amplified by the number of sets, adjusted for fitness, fatigue and conditions, and tied to settlement rules for retirements. Elo by surface gives a robust base; opponent-adjusted serve/return gives pair-specific hold/break; the market's sharp close is the benchmark.
match_winner.target: Winner of the match, with retirement/walkover per contract wording.

interactions.hypothesis: Counts scale with both rate and length, so favourites in short matches get fewer expected aces.
Altitude amplifies big servers' ace rate.
Wind raises count variance through in%.

Expected aces equal rate times service points, but the two are negatively correlated: a server with a high ace rate holds quickly, uses fewer points per game and wins faster, so the product is lower than the naive product for big servers.
Thin air reduces drag so the ball carries pace; players with high serve speed gain more in absolute ace probability than slower servers.
Wind lowers first-serve in-percentage on the windward end, which reduces aces there and raises double faults; the effect shows up as extra variance, not a mean shift.

A drop in first-serve speed over the last matches signals fatigue or an arm problem; a hurt server tends to protect the first serve (fewer aces) while the safer second serve may or may not keep the double-fault rate down, so the sign of the double-fault response depends on how the player adapts. The link is conditional on a speed-drop regime, not additive.
Raising first-serve pace raises ace given in but lowers in-percentage and adds second-serve points where double faults occur; aces and double faults move together with a non-monotone net effect.

player_aces_and_double_faults.label: Player aces and double faults
player_aces_and_double_faults.mechanism: Counts equal rates times opportunities: ace rate per service point (server ability, returner ability, surface, altitude, wind) times expected service points (closeness and format), with overdispersion from day-level first-serve variation. The official stats source and retirement rules define what counts.
player_aces_and_double_faults.target: Aces or double faults by a player in the match relative to a strike.

interactions.hypothesis: Heat raises retirement hazard more for older players.
Injured players start for first-round pay and retire more often.
Signals plus statements timestamp withdrawals.

Return time and event opportunities interact: a player expected back in four weeks can only return at an event whose entry deadline falls after he is cleared, so a slow recovery near a deadline removes a chance entirely.

A press statement that changes the stated plan switches the participation hazard from the base state to a near-certain state; signals before the statement raise the hazard continuously while the statement itself jumps it.

The contract outcome after a post-draw withdrawal depends on the definition of competing, so the hazard timeline is relevant only conditional on the rule that treats a withdrawal after the draw as No.

inputs.why: The game margin is the sum of break differentials over sets; a player who breaks more and holds more wins by larger margins, and the hold/break chain converts that into a spread distribution.
Spread cover depends on the specific pair's break rates, so opponent-adjusted components replace each player's raw averages.
The rating gap sets the expected margin; the mapping from Elo gap to expected game margin is roughly linear in the middle and flattens at the extremes.
Fat tails in the margin come from 6-0 and 6-1 sets; players with high lopsided-set rates cover large handicaps more often than a normal approximation says.
Sets are not independent: a player who wins the first set tends to win the second, so margins have a heavier spread than independent-set models give.
A handicap of -4.5 games means very different things in best-of-three and best-of-five; the set count and final-set rule set how large margins can get.
WTA matches have more breaks and smaller expected margins than ATP for the same rating gap, so ATP-calibrated models mis-size women's spreads.
A mid-match retirement leaves a partial margin that usually settles the favourite's cover as lost or void.
Whether a retired match settles the spread on games played, as a win for the other player, or as void changes the value of the cover side.
Spread rungs must be monotone and consistent with the winner price; violations indicate stale quotes rather than mispricing.
Game margins widen against a player with a weak second serve because they lose a higher share of their service games.
Pooling across surfaces stabilises margin estimates for players with few matches on the current surface.
Tired players lose more games late in matches, so fatigue widens margins in the final set more than it changes the winner.
Connects the hold model directly to the spread strike so mean and strike can be compared with the right variance.
Gives the exact discrete tail probabilities that a Gaussian approximation mis-sizes at half-point strikes.
Prevents treating the games spread as a shifted winner probability when a sizeable share of wins are close.
Provides the explicit within-set clustering that underlies heavy margin tails.
Quantifies the retirement tail for a spread contract whose retirement clause is cut off in the sample.

Shared definition with set_winner_and_any_set (single definition of the set-count and straight-set mass); supplies the set-differential rungs of KXATPSSPREAD (3-0/3-1 in best-of-five, 2-0 in best-of-three) that this archetype owns by target.

interactions.hypothesis: Game-differential tails come from lopsided sets, whose frequency exceeds iid predictions.
A retiring favourite leads in games but loses the match; settlement rules determine whether the spread counts.
Higher WTA break rates make spreads less sensitive to hold probability and more to return.

The expected margin scales with the number of games played, so the same hold gap produces a mean margin about 1.6 times larger in best-of-five than in best-of-three, but the straight-set stopping rule limits the increase.

Bagels and breadsticks concentrate in matches with a large rating gap, so the tail of margin grows faster than the mean as the gap increases; a player-level lopsided rate adds to this for the favourite.
With low hold levels (WTA) both players break often, so the margin variance is high but its mean depends on return strength more than on serve; with high holds (ATP) tiebreaks cap the margin.

In retirement matches the margin is truncated: either the contract settles on games played (favouring the leader's cover) or leaves the market for the unconditional clause, flipping which side of the strike a late-leading favourite lands on.
Both inputs create positive dependence at different scales (games within a set and sets within a match); together they determine the covariance of games across the match and the variance of D.

set_and_game_spreads.label: Set and game spreads
set_and_game_spreads.mechanism: Spreads depend on the distribution of the game (or set) differential, not just the win probability: it needs the hold/break probabilities of both players, the match format and the lopsidedness distribution. Push rules and half-point lines matter. Ladders of spread lines must be consistent with the match-winner market and with each other.
set_and_game_spreads.target: Game or set differential of a player relative to a handicap line.

inputs.why: Total games per set is driven by hold probabilities: two big servers hold often, push sets to 6-6 and raise totals, two weak servers trade breaks and shorten sets less predictably.

Some players produce bagels and breadsticks often; a high lopsided-set rate pulls totals under and is partly independent of the average rating gap.
Courts at a given event play consistently fast or slow; the event's past hold percentage is a stronger predictor of games per set than the generic surface label.
A retirement truncates a match and usually settles totals as under or void; the base rate (higher in best-of-five and for injured players) sets how much under-risk the over carries.
Whether a retired match counts games played, voids, or settles on a minimum set count changes the value of the over side.
Totals are listed at several strikes at once; the ladder must be monotonic in probability, so crossed or flat rungs flag stale quotes rather than information.
Serve and return point rates by surface feed the game-level Markov model that generates the distribution of games per set.
Tiebreak outcomes do not change the games count past 13 but do change set winners and match length; a player's tiebreak record is a weak, noisy trait.
Night sessions, a delayed start or a roof closing change conditions; indoor conditions raise hold rates and totals.

m.external_lines.label: Sportsbook/exchange reference prices
m.external_lines.measurement: For each match with a free-file close: p_book = two-way de-vig of Pinnacle close (power method: solve k so 1/o1^k... sums to 1; Shin only for 3-way sets; fall back to average close if Pinnacle missing). Compare to the Kalshi mid from the candlestick whose end time is the last one at or before the book file's stated close time; if the file gives no timestamp, use Kalshi last pre-start candle and label the comparison close-vs-close only. Output diff = kalshi_mid - p_book and sign persistence = share of consecutive matching snapshots with the same sign. Use for benchmarking only.
m.external_lines.mechanism: Sharp external prices are an information-rich prior; a Kalshi price that disagrees with the de-vigged sharp close either carries a stale quote or genuine information.
m.external_lines.rationale: The sharp closing line is the best-known single predictor in most sports markets, so any model must clear it, and its de-vigging method matters (proportional vs Shin vs power) especially for 3-way markets and long-shots. Subtle: timestamps must be matched; using a closing price against an earlier Kalshi quote overstates edge (look-ahead), and free historical files only give open/close snapshots.

ten.walkover_slot_hazard.rationale: The sampled rule sends non-occurrence to a fair price, so the exposure is to price drift in the final hours before a withdrawal becomes public, not to a final loss. Hazard varies by round, event tier and days since last match.

ten.win_margin_conversion_curve.label: Margin given win conversion curve
ten.win_margin_conversion_curve.measurement: From Sackmann scores compute for each edge bin P(D>k | winner) and P(D<0 | winner) by format; fit a logistic in edge and format; shrink to pooled values with n/(n+60). Combine with the winner probability: P(D>1.5)=P(win)*P(D>1.5|win)+P(lose)*P(D>1.5|lose). The edge bins use the market-free P(win) from the match_winner model (surface- and pace-adjusted Elo variant, stated in the dataset), never a price-implied probability.
ten.win_margin_conversion_curve.mechanism: The probability that a match winner also has a games margin above a threshold, as a function of pair edge and format.
ten.win_margin_conversion_curve.rationale: Spread settlement mixes winner and margin; the share of wins that are close (negative or small margins) rises as the gap shrinks and in best-of-five, and matters more than the mean margin at the strike.

ten.withdrawal_cascade_effect.label: Withdrawal cascade through the bracket
ten.withdrawal_cascade_effect.measurement: For each possible withdrawal, recompute title and stage probabilities with the replacement rules (lucky loser from qualifying draw with ratings, opponent's walkover with rest credit); weight by an empirical day-level withdrawal rate by round taken from W/O score rows (no timestamp; see tw_withdrawal_vintage and tw_sackmann_access), and treat any horizon-specific weighting as available only from forward own-capture; output the sensitivity of each player's title probability to the top-8 players' withdrawals.
ten.withdrawal_cascade_effect.mechanism: A withdrawal changes the bracket: the opponent gets a walkover (rest), a lucky loser enters, and the path of other players shifts.
ten.withdrawal_cascade_effect.rationale: The stage rule says a player who qualifies for the final but does not play still pays, so withdrawals at different points settle differently, and a withdrawal reshuffles the title probabilities of everyone else.

ten.withdrawal_hazard_timeline.rationale: The hazard is time-varying and clusters near the start; intervals carry different information, which determines when a market should move.

ten.within_match_dependence.label: Within-match dependence and momentum
ten.within_match_dependence.measurement: Estimate overdispersion by comparing observed games-per-set variance to the iid model; fit random match-form effect for spw; calibrate.
ten.within_match_dependence.mechanism: Point outcomes are not iid: serve alternation, pressure points and day-level form create correlation across points and sets.
ten.within_match_dependence.rationale: An iid-point Markov model understates variance in set and match outcomes; accounting for latent form shocks improves calibration for lopsided sets and straight-set sweeps. Subtle: true momentum effects are small; most dependence is latent form variation.

ten.within_match_serve_decay.label: Within-match serve and movement decay profile
ten.within_match_serve_decay.measurement: From Slam point-by-point compute spw_set_k per player in bo5 matches lasting >=3 sets; decay_k = spw_{k+1} - spw_k per player-match. Pooled mixed model decay ~ set_index + age>=33 + prior_match_minutes>200 + heat_flag + (1|player); player estimate = pooled prediction + player random effect shrunk n/(n+25) toward 0. Use only matches before as-of; report expected spw change by set index.
ten.within_match_serve_decay.mechanism: A player's serve-point win rate drifts down in later sets, and the drift differs by age, previous workload and match length.
ten.within_match_serve_decay.rationale: Late-set contracts (set 4, set 5, set 3 of a bo3) depend on fatigue effects that appear within the match rather than in rest days; a pre-match fatigue number only partly predicts it.
